What is a ground stop, and what kinds of flights can it apply to?

A ground stop is a process that keeps aircraft meeting specified criteria from departing. The criteria can be tied to an airport, a section of airspace, or aircraft/equipment categories, such as all departures to a certain airport, all flights entering a certain sector, or certain categories of aircraft headed to a destination.

How is ground speed defined in this glossary?
Ground speed is the speed of an aircraft relative to the earth’s surface.

When controllers conduct a handoff, what is being transferred and under what circumstances does it happen?

A handoff transfers an aircraft’s radar identification from one controller to another. It happens when the aircraft will enter the receiving controller’s airspace and radio communications with the aircraft will also be transferred.

How does the glossary distinguish HAA, HAL, and HAT?

HAA is the height of the minimum descent altitude above the published airport elevation, used with circling minimums. HAL is the height above a designated helicopter landing area for helicopter instrument approaches. HAT is the height of the decision height or minimum descent altitude above the highest runway elevation in the touchdown zone, used with straight-in minimums.

What information is included in hazardous weather information?

It includes summaries of major weather advisories such as SIGMETs, convective SIGMETs, urgent PIREPs, center weather advisories, AIRMETs, and G-AIRMETs. It also covers other significant developing conditions, like rapidly intensifying isolated thunderstorms or low ceilings and visibility becoming widespread, even if they are not yet in a current advisory.

How can forward military presence intended for deterrence end up escalating a situation instead?

Even if the actor sees a forward deployment as deterrent, an adversary may interpret it as hostile and react in kind. When the increase in presence is poorly calculated or not clearly signaled as non-aggressive, it can trigger counterproductive countermeasures and escalation.

What are military engagement activities, and what do they typically accomplish?

Military engagement activities include routine missions and continuing operations such as security cooperation and freedom of navigation. They help build partner relationships, improve regional awareness, expand knowledge of a partner nation’s capabilities and capacity, and can shape events in a favorable direction. They can also improve understanding of an adversary and provide warning of undesirable developments.

Under what circumstances can a military engagement activity grow into a larger operation?

A military engagement activity can expand when a situation deepens beyond routine engagement, such as limited support to counterinsurgency growing into a limited contingency operation. It can even become a major operation if the President commits US forces.

What does emergency preparedness include at the strategic level?

At the strategic level, emergency preparedness includes advance measures to reduce loss of life and property and protect national institutions from hazards through preparedness, mitigation, response, and recovery. It also includes planning like continuity of operations and continuity of government so DOD processes, procedures, and resources are ready to support the President and SecDef during a designated national security emergency.

How do continuity of operations and continuity of government differ?

Continuity of operations focuses on sustaining the functions, tasks, and duties needed to carry out military action or missions, including the commander’s responsibilities and staff support. Continuity of government is a coordinated effort across the executive, legislative, and judicial branches to preserve minimum essential government functions during a catastrophic emergency.

Why would people at a large music festival usually still be treated as uninvolved persons during UAS filming, even if the organizer announced the flight over speakers or mentioned it on tickets?
General announcements or notices do not make the crowd involved persons. Each individual must personally give permission and be made aware of the possible risks; otherwise they remain uninvolved.

What is meant by a controlled ground area in UAS operations?

A controlled ground area is the ground area where the UAS operator can ensure that only involved persons are present. It includes the flight geography area, the contingency area, and the ground risk buffer, and it may be protected by fencing or other suitable methods based on population density.

The operator must ensure that only involved persons are inside that area. The text says this can be done by using fencing or other appropriate protective methods, chosen with the local population density in mind.

How is maximum take-off mass defined for a UAS, and what must it cover?

Maximum take-off mass is the highest mass set by the manufacturer, or by the builder for a privately built UAS, that still ensures controllability and structural resistance within operational limits. It includes the airframe, motors, propellers if fitted, electronics and antennas, batteries, maximum fuel and fluids, and the heaviest approved payload with its sensors and supporting equipment.

What are the main responsibilities of an airspace observer during a UAS operation?

The airspace observer scans the surrounding airspace to detect collision risks with manned aircraft. They also keep track of the unmanned aircraft’s position, either visually or with electronic assistance, and warn the remote pilot about hazards while helping reduce or avoid negative effects.

What does UM155 tell the pilot, and what extra information may be included with it?
UM155 advises that ATS surveillance service has been established. It also requires a position, so the message may include the aircraft’s position as part of the radar contact advisory.

How is a MONITOR message different from a CONTACT message in these voice communication elements?

A CONTACT message instructs the flight crew to establish voice contact with the named ATS unit on the given frequency. A MONITOR message tells the crew only to listen on that frequency, and they are not required to make voice contact.

DISREGARD is used to tell the crew to ignore a previous uplink CPDLC message, but it must not be used for a clearance or instruction. Another element has to be added to make clear exactly which earlier message is to be ignored.

It asks the pilot to provide the remaining fuel as a time value and the number of persons on board. The chunk notes this message has an NE response attribute.

What is the difference between DM20 and DM21 for requesting voice contact?
Both are requests for voice contact, but DM20 is used when a frequency is not required in the message. DM21 is used when the frequency does need to be specified.

What wake-turbulence spacing must be added behind a Category A aircraft for different trailing categories?
Behind a Category A aircraft, add 3 minutes or 6 miles for Category B, C, or D; 3 minutes or 7 miles for Category E, F, or G; and 4 minutes or 8 miles for Category H or I.

Use an added interval of 3 minutes or 6 miles when a Category H or I aircraft follows a Category B, C, or D aircraft.

When must the trailing aircraft be told the lead aircraft’s manufacturer or model on a visual approach?

The trailing aircraft must be advised of the lead aircraft’s manufacturer or model whenever wake turbulence separation is required. The examples show this being done by naming the aircraft type in the traffic call.

How did the overtaking rule change for aircraft on final to closely spaced parallel runways?

The rule became broader. Instead of listing only super, heavy, B757, other large, and small combinations, it now prohibits any aircraft from overtaking another aircraft on final when wake turbulence separation is required and the parallel runways are less than 2,500 feet apart.

What does the updated weather guidance tell en route controllers to issue instead of specifically ARSR precipitation intensity?

It directs en route controllers to issue precipitation intensity generally, rather than limiting the wording to ARSR precipitation intensity. This reflects that the weather display now uses multiple data sources through WARP.

What headquarters elements are included in the Standing Joint Force Headquarters Group, and what are they meant to do?

It includes a one-star Joint Force Headquarters for horizon scanning, reconnaissance, liaison, and operational-level command and control in contingency planning and crisis response. It also includes the Standing Joint Force Logistic Component Headquarters to provide command, control, and core staff as the single joint logistics focus across crises, plus a one-star National Support Element Headquarters for multinational or NATO settings.

In this context, what does command and control need to accomplish when many relevant capabilities are owned by other actors?

Command and control cannot rely only on direct authority when key assets belong to others with their own objectives. Instead, the commander may need to achieve effects by aligning multiple actors around a shared purpose, while still understanding the context, expressing intent, guiding planning, and setting freedoms and constraints.

How should a commander operate in multi-domain operations to make command and control effective?

They should enable stronger data collection and information sharing, and ensure subordinate commanders have agile, adaptable multi-domain capabilities with the necessary authorities and resilience. Commanders and staffs must then synchronize and orchestrate capabilities from all domains so effects converge at decisive points.

Why is national veto such an important issue in coalition operations?

A national contingent commander can block an order they believe conflicts with national interests. Because coalition operations are politically sensitive and contributing governments may be risk-averse, this possibility can significantly shape planning and execution.

What kinds of national limitations can restrict a joint task force's freedom of action in a multinational operation?

Limits can come from different views of the mission, different national interpretations of command authority, and national rules on the use of force that may differ from the force commander's guidance. They can also arise from varying interpretations of the law of armed conflict, different attitudes to force protection and risk, and targeting processes that require coalition-wide agreement.

Why were systems like the Stugna-P mainly kept with Ukraine’s existing ground forces, while Javelin and NLAW could be spread more broadly?

The main factor was training burden. Stugna-P and other wire-guided systems took substantial training to use well, with crews needing about 30 days of preparation, so they stayed largely with established ground-force units. Javelin could be taught in days and NLAW in hours, which made them easier to distribute more widely.

How did Ukraine prepare anti-tank crews to employ the Stugna-P effectively before the full-scale invasion?

After 2014, Ukraine invested heavily in anti-tank training and created a School of Anti-Tank Artillery at the 184th Training Centre of the National Academy of Ground Forces. Crews arriving from military units underwent about 30 days of training to become proficient with the Stugna-P.

What additional capability made the Javelin command launch unit especially useful for special forces and other specialist troops?

Its command launch unit had uses beyond firing missiles, including intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Because of that added utility, Javelin systems were prioritized for special forces and other specialist formations.

What early problem affected Western-supplied anti-tank guided weapons in Ukrainian service, and how was it addressed?

Rapid training for new units often neglected maintenance, especially battery upkeep, so many Western-supplied ATGWs were initially unusable when issued. The problem was reduced over time once the proper maintenance instructions were circulated.

How did improvements in Ukraine’s radar network contribute to Russian tactical errors in radio-electronic attack?

Ukraine had reorganized and upgraded its air-defence warning system after 2014, including radars with longer detection ranges, better accuracy, faster processing, and quicker deployment. Because Russian forces had not fully appreciated these improvements, they misjudged Ukrainian air-defence capability and made mistakes in how they employed electronic attack.

What is the Air Operations Center's role within the Theater Air Control System, and how does it function when the COMAFFOR is also the JFACC?

The AOC is the senior element and main command-and-control node of the TACS, with the personnel and equipment needed to plan and conduct air operations. When the COMAFFOR also serves as the JFACC, the AOC functions as a joint AOC and is normally the headquarters where the JFC’s draft joint integrated prioritized target list is built from component target nominations. It also receives air support requests for CAS, which starts the AOC’s allocation process for close air support.

How does the Control and Reporting Center support CAS and AI missions during execution?

For CAS, the CRC can pass current situation updates from the ASOC to inbound aircraft and relay battle damage assessment from departing aircraft back to the ASOC. For AI, it can send updates from earlier AI missions to aircraft entering the area so they have better situational awareness. More broadly, it manages air component missions as directed in the air tasking order.

Why is AWACS often the first tactical C2 element to arrive in theater, and what responsibilities does it take on early in the campaign?

AWACS usually arrives first because it can immediately provide air surveillance, identify airborne objects, and control air operations. It gives the air component commander a deep-look capability for both offensive and defensive air operations, along with low-level and extended radio coverage. Until the CRC is established, AWACS serves as the AOC’s primary tactical command-and-control extension.

What is the ASOC, where is it typically aligned, and what can it become when co-located with a division?

The ASOC is the TACS’s primary control agency for executing airpower in direct support of land operations. It is a direct subordinate of the AOC and is normally aligned with the Army echelon above brigade that is best able to integrate fires, effects, and procedural control. When co-located with a division, it can form the JAGIC by integrating with division fires, airspace, air and missile defense, and aviation elements.

What employment principles for an ASOC are highlighted in the text, and what is the reasoning behind them?

The text says an ASOC should not be split except when relocating, because its effectiveness comes from a trained team working together. It also should be placed in a relatively secure location, since losing it to enemy action would significantly reduce support to friendly ground forces. At the same time, planners must balance security with radio range and communications limits.

What does an outer marker do on an ILS approach, and where is it usually located?

An outer marker is a marker beacon placed at or near the glideslope intercept altitude for an ILS. It normally sits about 4 to 7 miles from the runway threshold on the extended runway centerline and sends a distinctive aural and visual signal to equipped aircraft.

How is an aircraft treated when it flies an overhead maneuver, and when is its IFR flight plan canceled?
An overhead maneuver is treated as a VFR operation, not an IFR approach. The IFR flight plan is canceled when the aircraft reaches the initial point on the maneuver’s initial approach segment.

What are the normal elements of an overhead maneuver pattern?

The pattern normally includes required radio contact, a specified speed, and an initial approach of 3 to 5 miles. It also uses an elliptical pattern with two 180-degree turns, a defined break point, the direction of turns, an altitude at least 500 feet above the conventional pattern, and a rollout on final at least one-quarter mile from the threshold and at least 300 feet above the ground.

In terminal-area ATC use, what is an outer fix and how is it normally used?

In terminal operations, an outer fix is a fix in the terminal area other than the final approach fix. Aircraft are usually cleared to it by a center or approach control facility, then cleared onward from there to the final approach fix or final approach course.

What is performance-based navigation under ICAO terminology?

Performance-based navigation is area navigation built around defined performance requirements for aircraft flying an ATS route, an instrument approach, or within designated airspace. Those requirements are expressed through navigation specifications such as RNAV or RNP and include factors like accuracy, integrity, continuity, availability, and needed functionality.

How would a controller instruct an aircraft to cross a named position at a specific time and altitude, and what does that instruction mean?

The message format is to direct the aircraft to cross the position at the stated time and altitude. In plain language, it tells the crew to be over that fix at that exact time while at the assigned altitude.

What is the difference between the crossing messages that use 'AT OR BEFORE' and 'AT OR AFTER' for time?

The 'AT OR BEFORE' version requires the aircraft to cross the specified position no later than the stated time. The 'AT OR AFTER' version requires the crossing to occur no earlier than the stated time.

There are three speed-related crossing formats: cross the position at a stated speed, at or less than a stated speed, or at or greater than a stated speed. These cover exact, maximum, and minimum speed constraints respectively.

What do the 'EXPECT speed' uplink messages do when tied to a time, position, or altitude?

They serve as advance notice that a speed instruction may later take effect at the stated time, position, or altitude. Some versions also notify the crew that a speed range, rather than a single speed, may be issued.

What is the primary objective of homeland operations, and what kinds of activities do they include?

The main objective is to defend the United States from attack. Homeland operations include planning and execution to detect, preempt, respond to, mitigate, and recover from the full range of threats and incidents affecting the homeland, whether natural or manmade.

How does the text define compellence, and what is it trying to achieve against an adversary?

Compellence is the use of military force to make an adversary change ongoing behavior or do something it would prefer not to do. Its purpose is to influence the opponent so the perceived cost of resisting becomes too high.

What forms can compellence take, and how does airpower support each of them?

Compellence can take the form of denial, risk, punishment, or a combination of these. Airpower supports denial by using persistent ISR and precision attack against fielded forces, supports risk by putting valued strategic targets under credible threat, and supports punishment by lawfully striking military targets across the adversary’s system with discrimination.

What is paralysis in this context, and why is airpower especially suited to create it?

Paralysis is described as a type of denial that uses parallel attacks across the enemy’s whole system, including leadership and command and control, to leave the enemy unable to control key systems or even broader society. Airpower is particularly effective because it can hit a very wide set of targets quickly and throughout the operational environment.

What Air Force capabilities are highlighted for homeland operations and defense support of civil authorities?

The text highlights control of the air, rapid global mobility, global ISR, and command and control. These capabilities enable the Air Force to conduct homeland operations and support civil authorities when required.

What does OSO #07 require the remote crew to verify during a product inspection of the UAS?

The remote crew must ensure the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation and that it matches the approved concept of operations. The inspection is meant to confirm consistency between the actual UAS and how it is intended to be used.

How do the assurance expectations for product inspection procedures change from low to high?

At low assurance, the inspection is documented and takes the manufacturer’s recommendations into account when available. At medium, the same applies but the inspection is recorded with checklists. At high, those documented checklist-based procedures must also be validated by the competent authority or a body designated by it.

What is meant by 'external systems supporting the UAS operation' in this text?

These are systems not already part of the UAS but used to launch or take off, perform pre-flight checks, or keep the aircraft within its operational volume. Examples include GNSS, satellite systems, air traffic management, and U-space services. Systems only activated after loss of control are not included.

What minimum topics must operational procedures cover for the proposed operation?

They must address flight planning, pre- and post-flight inspections, assessment of environmental conditions before and during the mission, actions for unexpected adverse conditions, normal operations, contingency actions, emergency actions, and occurrence reporting. The limitations of any supporting external systems also need to be defined in the operations manual.

How does the text distinguish complex operational procedures from simple ones?

Complex procedures are those that can strain the crew’s ability to respond by increasing workload or coordination with outside entities such as air traffic management. A higher-complexity example is when contingency or emergency actions require the remote pilot to take manual control of an otherwise automated UAS. Simple procedures are the opposite and do not create that level of burden.

What does the text identify as the main doctrinal issue for unmanned and remotely piloted aircraft systems?
It identifies interoperability as the central doctrinal issue. The aircraft should be treated as part of a wider ISR enterprise that can both cue and be cued by other collection and PED capabilities.

In this context, what is an ISR request and what is a JISR result?

An ISR request is a formal request from operations staff to start ISR collection using a specified capability or asset in support of prioritized mission requirements. A JISR result is the output of the JISR process that is passed back to the requester in the required format.

How should Watchkeeper be tasked and represented for other users' awareness?

Watchkeeper should not be tasked through the normal air tasking order process. Its employment needs a flexible and agile tasking approach, and although it may not be planned on the same timeline or in the same detail as manned assets, it should still be annotated on the ATO like other land-assigned assets, with details appended for visibility.

Why does the text say effective ISR operations depend on interoperability?

Because the UAS collect function is only one part of a larger intelligence cycle that begins with a request and ends with a JISR result. To be effective, the capability must work smoothly with the systems and activities that task it and that process, exploit, and disseminate what it collects.

How are Black Hornet, Desert Hawk III, and Class I aircraft employed and overseen at the tactical level?

Black Hornet is tasked and used at the lowest tactical level, within company or platoon formations. Desert Hawk III is deployed with tactical command given to the supported formations and units. Even though Class I aircraft data is analysed and exploited locally in real time, headquarters staff still need awareness of which assets are in theatre and how and where they are being used.

When should sequenced flashing lights be operated for a runway approach lighting system?

Use sequenced flashing lights when visibility is under 3 miles and instrument approaches are being made to the runway served by that approach lighting system. They may also be operated if a pilot asks for them or whenever the controller considers them necessary, as long as that does not conflict with the pilot’s request.

What is the relationship between sequenced flashing lights and the approach lighting system?
Sequenced flashing lights are part of the approach lighting system itself. Because of that, they cannot be used when the associated approach lighting system is turned off.

How should MALSR or ODALS be set when they have separate on-off and intensity controls?

They are normally operated using the visibility-based settings in the two lighting tables for day and night conditions. However, those settings can be changed if local directives require different levels for atmospheric, terrain, or twilight conditions, if a pilot requests a setting, or if the controller judges another setting is needed and the pilot has not asked otherwise.
